series.name: The Comment Section
series.concept: Each episode starts with a single Instagram comment — the kind you've seen a thousand times — and spirals into a full story. Meta, funny, self-aware, and incredibly shareable.

episodes.title: Bhai Ye Filter Hai Ya Asli?

slides.text: The comment: 'Bhai ye filter hai ya asli? 😂' 47 likes. Posted under Priya's selfie. But what if we actually answered that question? Honestly?
Priya's morning routine: Wake up. Wash face. Moisturizer. Foundation. Concealer. Contour. Highlight. Set it. Then open the camera. Smooth filter. Warm tone. One photo out of 47 attempts.
Layer 1: Her actual face. Layer 2: Makeup. Layer 3: Lighting. Layer 4: Phone beauty mode. Layer 5: Instagram filter. Layer 6: Manual editing. You're looking at version 6.0 of a human face.
The guy who commented 'filter hai ya asli?' — his profile pic has a beard filter, a sigma male preset, and a gym mirror selfie with contrast at 200%. Bhai, TU asli hai?
We're all filtering. She uses beauty filters. He uses sigma filters. Your food photo has saturation +40. Nobody's posting 'asli' on Instagram. And that's okay. Just don't pretend you are.

episodes.synopsis: Someone comments 'Filter hai ya asli?' — a story about beauty standards, Instagram vs reality, and why we can't tell real from fake anymore.
episodes.caption: "Filter hai ya asli?" — posted by a guy whose profile pic has a sigma male filter. We're ALL filtering. What's your most-used filter? 😂

episodes.title: First!

slides.text: The comment: 'FIRST! 🔥🔥🔥' Posted 3 seconds after a celebrity's photo. 2 likes. Zero replies. But Rahul was happy. He was first. First at what? First at nothing.

Rahul has notifications ON for 43 accounts. The moment they post, he drops everything. Types 'First!' Average response time: 4.2 seconds. Faster than Zomato delivery. Slower than meaningful connection.
Why do we want to be first? Same reason kids raise hands in class. Same reason we honk 0.3 seconds after the light turns green. Being first = being seen.
Nobody has ever gotten a job because they commented 'First.' Nobody fell in love because of it. The celebrity doesn't see it. But Rahul feels something. For 3 seconds.
Plot twist: You're reading this post right now. Someone in the comments has already typed 'First!' Go check. They're there. They're always there. Respect the grind.

episodes.synopsis: Why does being first get you? A story about the desperate need to be noticed in a world of 2 billion users.
episodes.caption: "First!" — The comment that means nothing but feels like everything. Tag that friend who does this on EVERY post 😂

episodes.title: Bhai Location Batao

slides.text: The comment: 'Bhai location batao 📍🔥' Posted under a reel of turquoise water. 127 likes. Enthusiastic. Urgent. Like they're booking the flight now. Spoiler: They're not.
Arjun has 847 saved reels in 'Travel Goals 🌍'. Bali. Ladakh. Santorini. He knows the exact hotel in each reel. He's never been to any of them.
Time spent saving travel reels: 45 hours/year. Time spent planning a trip: 0. Budget saved for travel: ₹0. Reels about Goa: 200+. Times been to Goa: Zero.
Saving a reel feels like doing something. 'I'll go someday.' Someday is where dreams go to retire.
Open your saved reels. Pick ONE location. Book it this month. Even if it's 4 hours by bus. Stop saving. Start going.

episodes.synopsis: Every travel reel gets 'Location batao.' But do they actually go? A story about the gap between saving reels and living.
episodes.caption: "Bhai location batao" — asked on 200 reels. Went to zero locations. What's the first saved location you see? Drop it 👇

episodes.title: Iska BF/GF Kaun Hai?

slides.text: The comment: 'Iska bf kaun hai yaar? 💔' Posted under a girl's dance reel by a guy who has never spoken to her. Doesn't know her name. But needs to know her relationship status. Urgently.
Think about this in real life. A stranger dancing at a party. You walk up to her friend: 'Bhai iska boyfriend kaun hai?' You'd get a weird look. Online? 200 likes.
It's called a parasocial relationship. You feel like you know someone because you watch their content. But they don't know you exist. Hard to hear. Still true.
But sometimes the comment section is beautiful. 'He's lucky whoever he is.' 'Queen doesn't need a king.' 'Bhai apna kaam kar.' The internet correcting itself. Rare, but it happens.
Next time you're about to type 'iska bf kaun hai' — would you say this to their face? If no, don't type it. The comment section is someone's space. Act like a guest.

episodes.synopsis: Every attractive person's post gets the same comment. A story about parasocial relationships and entitlement.
episodes.caption: "Iska bf kaun hai?" — asked by 10,000 strangers who will never meet her. What's the most unhinged comment you've seen? 👇

episodes.title: Song Name?

slides.text: The comment: 'Song name please? 🎵' The song name is literally at the bottom of the reel. In bold. With the artist name. But Kunal didn't see it. Because Kunal doesn't read. Kunal scrolls.
Average time on a reel: 3-7 seconds. We don't watch content. We let it wash over us. Then we ask questions it already answered.
'Song name?' is the beginning. 'What app?' (Says Canva on screen). 'Where is this?' (Location tag right there). We've outsourced reading to the comment section.
Sometimes the audio name is 'originalaudioxyz_remix_v3_final_FINAL.' Fair enough. Kunal gets a pass.
Before you comment 'Song name?' — look at the bottom. Tap the audio. Check description. 3 seconds. Less time than typing the question. Revolutionary.

episodes.synopsis: The song name is ON the reel. And still — 'Song name please?' A story about how we've stopped reading.
episodes.caption: The song name is ON the reel. In bold. With a link. "Song name please?" 😂 Tag someone who does this under EVERY reel 👇

episodes.title: Photoshop Hai

slides.text: The comment: 'Photoshop hai bro 😂' Under a genuinely stunning sunset. The photographer spent 3 hours waiting. But Ankit, from bed at 2 AM, declared it fake.
Step 1: See something impressive. Step 2: Feel inadequate. Step 3: Declare it fake. Step 4: Feel better. The comment isn't about the photo. It's about protecting your ego.
The same person uses 3 filters on their chai photo. Adjusts brightness on their bike selfie. But THAT'S not editing. That's 'aesthetic.'
We've seen so much fake that we can't be impressed by real things. Real talent? 'Auto-tune.' Real body? 'Steroids.' Cynicism is the laziest form of intelligence.
Next time something impresses you — try 'Wow, this is incredible.' No investigation. Just appreciation. It's free. And it makes the internet slightly less terrible.

episodes.synopsis: Any impressive photo gets 'Photoshop hai.' A story about how we've become so cynical we can't believe anything real.
episodes.caption: "Photoshop hai" — the comment that protects your ego from admiring someone else's work. Have you been that person? 😂

episodes.title: Nobody: Literally Nobody:

slides.text: The comment: 'Nobody: Literally nobody: Not a single soul: This guy: *does the thing*' Funny in 2018. Still here in 2026. The cockroach of internet humor.
The format worked for highlighting absurdity. Then people added layers. The joke got a joke extension pack.
'Nobody: Me at 3 AM: eating Maggi.' That's not how the format works. You eating Maggi doesn't need a 'nobody.' We all do. It's not absurd.
Memes die in weeks. This one survived 8 years. It's the Maggi of memes — basic, reliable, impossible to replace.
Let it live. Before 'Nobody:' it was 'That's what she said.' Before that, 'Your mom.' The format changes. The laziness is eternal.

episodes.synopsis: The most overused meme format. A story about how internet humor evolves and refuses to die.
episodes.caption: Nobody: Literally nobody: This meme format: *refuses to die since 2018* What's the most overused comment you see? 👇

episodes.title: Crying in the Club

slides.text: The comment: 'I'm literally crying in the club rn 😭😭😭' Posted at 1:47 AM. On a Tuesday. Deepak is not in a club. He's in bed. In boxers. With Kurkure. Not crying.
Internet translation: 'Crying' = slightly amused. 'Literally dead' = mildly entertained. 'I can't breathe' = exhaled through nose. 'SCREAMING' = smiled. Nothing means what it says.
2010: 'lol' meant you laughed. 2025: 'lol' means 'I'm mildly annoyed but don't want to fight.' Language inflation is real.
'That was nice' gets 0 engagement. 'I'M LITERALLY DECEASED' gets 47 likes. The internet rewards exaggeration.
When's the last time you were ACTUALLY crying in a club? We've made every emotion a 10. What do we use when something actually hits?

episodes.synopsis: 'Crying in the club rn 😭' — posted from bed at 1:47 AM, while eating chips. A story about performative emotions.
episodes.caption: "Crying in the club" at 1:47 AM from bed. With Kurkure. What emotion do you fake the most online? 😂

episodes.title: Bhai Gym Jaa

slides.text: The comment: 'Bhai gym jaa 💪' Posted under a guy sharing his PAINTING. His art. Not his body. But gym jaa. Because gym fixes everything. Apparently.
Sad? Gym jaa. Broke? Gym jaa. Heartbroken? Gym jaa. Lost your wallet? Gym jaa. Grandmother passed? Gym jaa bro, she would've wanted it.
2020: Gym bro culture merged with sigma male culture. Deadlifts could cure depression. Bench press fixed your CIBIL score. Protein shake was therapy.
Exercise IS good for mental health. That's true. But using it as a response to someone's art? That's not advice. That's a script.
If your first thought is 'bhai itna text padh liya, ab gym jaa' — you're exactly who this episode is about. Fair enough. Let's both go. After this reel.

episodes.synopsis: 'Gym jaa bro' — the answer to every question, every emotion. A story about how gym became universal advice.
episodes.caption: "Gym jaa bro" — the answer to every question. Is gym the new therapy or just the laziest comment? Drop your best moment 💪

episodes.title: Who's Watching in 2026?

slides.text: The comment: 'Who's watching this in 2026? 🙋‍♂️ Like if you're here!' Under a 2014 Honey Singh song. 847 likes. Listening to an old song in the current year is apparently an achievement.
It's an identity signal. 'I listen to OLD music' is a flex. A nostalgia badge. You didn't discover anything — the algorithm suggested it to everyone.
2016: 'Who's here in 2016?' 2020: 'Lockdown brought me here.' 2026: 'Gen Z doesn't know about this.' Bro, Gen Z MADE this viral.
But here's the beautiful part. Strangers bonding over a shared song across years. It's silly. But it's kind of pure.
Keep commenting. It's harmless. In 2035, someone will see YOUR comment and think 'People were vibing in 2026 too.' You just made history. Sort of.

episodes.synopsis: The time-stamp comment under every old video. Nostalgia, identity, and the bizarre habit of announcing when you're watching.
episodes.caption: "Who's watching in 2026?" — under every video from 2014. What's the oldest video you've commented on? 👇

episodes.title: This Is So Me

slides.text: 'This is SO me 😂😂😂' Under someone confidently roasting their boss. Meera hasn't made eye contact with her boss in 3 months. But yeah. 'So her.'
'This is so me' under a gym reel = 'I went once in 2019.' Under travel = 'I want this to be me.' Under cooking = 'I boiled pasta successfully.' Aspirational, not accurate.
Aspirational self-tagging. You identify with who you WANT to be. So you claim the content. Build an online identity 3 promotions ahead of reality.
Maybe that's okay? 'This is so me' is manifesting. Seeing yourself as something better is the first step to becoming it.
Comment 'This is so me' under that 5 AM routine video. You woke up at 11. But aspiration is free. Maybe tomorrow it WILL be you. Probably not. But maybe.

episodes.synopsis: 'This is so me' under a video of someone doing a backflip. You can't do a backflip. Aspirational identity online.
episodes.caption: "This is so me" under a 5 AM routine. You woke up at noon. Aspiration is free 😂 Tag someone who does this 👇

episodes.title: Not Me at 3 AM

slides.text: 'Not me reading this at 3 AM instead of sleeping 😅' 342 likes. 342 people also awake at 3 AM. Reading comments about not sleeping. The irony is thick.
Plan: Check one notification at 11:30. Reality: 47 reels, 3 Twitter threads, 2 Reddit holes, Wikipedia page about how dolphins sleep with one eye open. Time: 3:17 AM.
Social media is designed for infinite scrolling. No endpoint. The scroll is a slot machine. Each pull MIGHT give something amazing. Usually a cat video. You pull again.
We set alarms. Put the phone across the room. Get up, get it, 'just check one thing.' The phone has more pull than gravity.
If you're reading this at 3 AM — hi. We see you. Millions of us scrolling. A support group nobody signed up for. Put the phone down. You won't. But I tried.

episodes.synopsis: The most self-aware comment on the internet. The epidemic of late-night scrolling.
episodes.caption: If you're reading this at 3 AM — put the phone down. You won't. What time are you actually reading this? Drop your timestamp 👇

episodes.title: Unfollow Kar Lo

slides.text: 'Bhai teri last 5 reels same concept hai.' Reply: 'Pasand nahi toh unfollow kar lo.' Translation: 'I have no response to valid criticism so I'm choosing violence.'
Hateful comment? Valid. Constructive feedback? Cowardice. Mild joke? Overreaction. Using it for everything is the problem.
'Unfollow kar lo' ends every conversation. Online equivalent of 'main tere baap ka naukar nahi hoon.' Debate over. Logic optional.
Creators who grow read feedback. 'Your last 5 reels are the same' is free market research. Blocking feedback means staying the same forever.
Read every comment. Respond to helpful ones. Ignore hateful ones. Save 'Unfollow kar lo' for the truly toxic. Not for the person who said your audio was too loud.

episodes.synopsis: 'Don't like it? Unfollow.' The nuclear option. A story about replacing criticism with blocking.
episodes.caption: "Unfollow kar lo" — the reply that ends every argument. Power move or cope? Drop your take 👇

episodes.title: Who Came From [Creator]?

slides.text: 'Who else came here from Tanmay Bhat's video? 🙋‍♂️' 523 likes. HOW you arrived is apparently content-worthy. Nobody cares, but everyone announces.
Big creator mentions small creator → 1,000 new followers in an hour. All commenting 'I'm from Tanmay.' Like tourists with matching t-shirts.
Shoutout economy: ₹5,000-50,000 for one story mention. The comment 'From [creator]' is proof of purchase.
'I follow Tanmay' = 'I have good taste.' 'I found this on explore' = 'I'm an algorithm's pawn.' Nobody wants to be the pawn.
The algorithm sent you to Tanmay's video too. You didn't choose it. We all came from the algorithm. Welcome to the Matrix.

episodes.synopsis: The shoutout economy and why we announce HOW we found something.
episodes.caption: "Who came from Tanmay's video?" — as if arriving is an accomplishment. Where did YOU come from? 😂

episodes.title: Ratio

slides.text: 'Ratio.' No argument. No logic. Just the word. If enough people like the reply more than the post — the poster is publicly defeated.
Ratio is the internet's guillotine. You don't need to be right. Just more liked. Democracy at its most chaotic. The mob decides truth.
Ratio doesn't mean you're wrong. It means you're unpopular. A scientist posting 'earth is round' can be ratioed by a joke. Popularity ≠ correctness.
Professional ratio-ers: follow controversial accounts, wait for hot take, type 'Ratio' in 0.5 seconds. A sport. No thinking required.
Next time you see 'Ratio' — is the post actually wrong? Or just unpopular? Those are very different things.

episodes.synopsis: One word. The internet's quickest judgment. When a reply gets more likes than the original.
episodes.caption: "Ratio" — one word that decides arguments. No logic needed. Have you been ratioed? Or done the ratioing? 👇

episodes.title: Link in Bio?

slides.text: 'Where can I buy this?' Reply: 'Link in bio! 🔗' Bio has a Linktree with 47 dead links. The one you need? 404.
Instagram: no links in captions. Creators: 'Link in bio!' Users: leave post, go to bio, open Linktree, find link, forget why they came.
'Link in bio for FREE template!' Click: WhatsApp group → Telegram → ₹4,999 course. The template doesn't exist.
1-3% of people check. Half bounce from Linktree. 80% don't buy. 1,000 mentions for 2-3 conversions. But they keep saying it.
The day Instagram allows links in captions, 'Link in bio' dies and millions of Linktrees become digital fossils. Until then — just DM them.

episodes.synopsis: The Linktree graveyard and the broken promise economy of Instagram.
episodes.caption: "Link in bio!" — the biggest lie on Instagram since 2016. When's the last time it actually worked? 😂

episodes.title: Tag Someone

slides.text: 'Tag someone who needs to see this ❤️' Simran tags Neha. Neha tags Pooja. Nobody reads the post. Relay race where nobody knows what they're running for.
Each tag = free reach. Your tag is their marketing. You think you're sharing. They think '2x impressions free.' Both can be true.
'Tag someone you can't live without.' 'Tag your bestie.' Your bestie is sitting next to you. Just show them the phone.
You've been tagged today. Did you check? 70% of tags go unchecked. Swiped away. They'll never know. Bliss.
Sometimes a tag is a love language. 'This reminded me of you.' When the right person tags the right thing — it's a tiny warm moment. Keep tagging. Just skip the giveaways.

episodes.synopsis: The modern chain letter of Instagram. Why we tag and whether they look.
episodes.caption: "Tag someone" — do you check when tagged? Or swipe the notification away? Be honest 😂

episodes.title: Main Character Energy

slides.text: 'Bro thinks he's the main character 💀💀' Under a video of a guy walking confidently through a market. Just... walking. With good posture. That's cringe now.
2020: 'Main character energy' was a compliment. 2024: It's an insult. Same phrase, opposite meaning. The vibe shift.
When did confidence become cringe? He's living his life. You're judging his walk from bed. Who's actually winning?
'Main character' is cope. 'I'm uncomfortable with someone having more confidence.' Instead of leveling up, we pull down. Crabs in a bucket.
Walk like you're in a movie. Dance in public. The people calling you 'main character' are NPCs of their own story. You ARE the main character. Of your life. That's literally how life works.

episodes.synopsis: When did confidence become cringe? Who benefits from keeping you small?
episodes.caption: "Main character" — said by someone watching from bed at 2 PM. Be YOUR main character. What's the most main-character thing you've done? 💪

episodes.title: Editing Sikha De

slides.text: 'Bhai editing kaise ki? App batao na! 🔥' Creator spent 6 hours. Learned After Effects over 2 years. But sure — it's about the app.
Asking 'which app?' is like asking a chef 'which stove?' The stove didn't make biryani. 15 years of practice did.
The app doesn't matter. CapCut, Premiere, DaVinci — all can make great content. The difference: 500 hours of practice and willingness to be bad first.
We see the 15-second reel, not the 6 hours. So we think 'easy app.' It's not the app. It's never the app.
Download CapCut. Free. Now make a reel as good. You can't? That's 500 hours of practice you haven't done. Start or keep asking.

episodes.synopsis: 'App batao na!' — confusing the tool with the talent.
episodes.caption: "Editing kaise ki? App batao!" CapCut is free. Go make something as good. What skill are YOU shortcutting? 😂

episodes.title: Overrated

slides.text: 'Overrated.' Under a Messi highlight. Under a Coldplay concert. Under wedding photos. Nothing safe from the person who thinks popularity = bad.
'Overrated' means 'too many people like this, so I can't.' Not a review — a reflex. Popularity triggers contrarians like a red cloth triggers a bull. Except the bull is in bed at 1 AM.
Things 'overrated': Messi. Kohli. Travel. Friends. Love. Happiness. At this point, breathing is overrated.
Some people build identity on disliking popular things. 'I don't watch mainstream.' Cool. What DO you like? Silence.
Instead of 'Overrated' — try 'Not for me.' Same meaning, less arrogance. One makes you a critic. The other makes you human.

episodes.synopsis: 'Overrated.' Zero explanation. Posted under everything popular. Contrarianism as personality.
episodes.caption: "Overrated" — says more about you than the content. What have you called overrated but secretly enjoy? 😂

episodes.title: Apni Aukat Mein Reh

slides.text: 'Bhai apni aukat mein reh 😂' Under a small-town boy's video about wanting to move to Mumbai. He's 19. Dreams of filmmaking. Someone told him to know his place.
'Aukat' is India's favorite gatekeeping tool. Not enough money? Aukat. Wrong college? Aukat. It's a cage built by people who never left their own.
Dhirubhai — petrol pump attendant. Rajinikanth — bus conductor. Nawazuddin — watchman. Every success story is someone who didn't listen to 'aukat mein reh.'
The person who says 'aukat mein reh' is never at the top. They're in the middle — terrified someone from below might pass them. Your ambition is their mirror.
If someone says 'apni aukat mein reh' — screenshot it. Work in silence. When you make it, post the screenshot as a carousel. Best reply: results.

episodes.synopsis: 'Stay in your lane.' The comment designed to cage dreamers.
episodes.caption: "Apni aukat mein reh" — said to every dreamer. Who said this to you? How did you prove them wrong? 👇

episodes.title: L

slides.text: 'L' Under a guy's post about his startup failing after 2 years. Two years of work. One letter. Not 'what happened?' Just L.
The internet has two outcomes: W or L. No middle ground. No 'it was complicated.' Nuance? That's an L too.
Got dumped? L. Song didn't go viral? L. Tried and failed? L. The internet decided trying and failing is worse than never trying.
Every success is built on a graveyard of Ls. Ambani's first business failed. Bachchan went bankrupt. Their Ls became their story.
Next time someone shares a failure — comment anything except 'L.' An L from your keyboard costs nothing. But it might cost them their courage.

episodes.synopsis: 'L.' One letter. The internet's quickest judgment. A story about reducing human experiences to wins and losses.
episodes.caption: "L" — one letter dismissing years of effort. What's an L that made you stronger? Share it 👇

episodes.title: Fake

slides.text: 'Fake.' Under a video of a man giving food to homeless people. 'Only for the camera.' Maybe. Or maybe he fed 50 people and you fed 0.
Sometimes it IS fake. Staged pranks. Scripted drama. Enough fake content to make cynicism reasonable. But we've gone too far. Everything's fake until proven real.
When you call real charity 'Fake', you discourage future charity. When you call tears 'Fake', you punish vulnerability. Cycle of cynicism.
Before commenting 'Fake': Did someone get helped? Was something good done? If yes, does it matter if a camera was rolling?
The 'Fake' commenter has never posted anything real themselves. No vulnerability. No charity. Easy to judge from the sidelines.

episodes.synopsis: 'Fake.' Posted under charity, success stories, apologies. The erosion of trust online.
episodes.caption: "Fake" — the accusation that costs nothing but discourages everything genuine. Most real thing you've seen online? 👇

episodes.title: Plot Twist

slides.text: 'Plot twist: it's scripted 😂' Under a wholesome kid surprising his mom. 47 people liked it. Being the 'smart one' who sees through things is addictive.
Pointing out something's scripted makes us feel smart. Cheapest way to feel intelligent — not creating, but deconstructing.
Everything you enjoy is scripted. Movies. Stand-up. That emotional ad. You don't comment 'Breaking Bad is scripted.' Because it was never about truth. It was about superiority.
The 'Plot twist' commenter gets joy from ruining someone's experience. A tiny power trip at someone else's expense.
Plot twist: you're still reading. It's scripted. Obviously. But did it make you think? If yes — scripted or not, it worked. Let things work on you.

episodes.synopsis: 'Plot twist: it's scripted 😂' — ruining every story. The need to be the smartest in the comments.
episodes.caption: "Plot twist: scripted!" — the comment that thinks it's clever. Do you let yourself enjoy things? 👇

episodes.title: The Good Comment

slides.text: 24 episodes of chaos. 'First!' 'Fake!' 'L.' 'Overrated.' We've seen the worst. But here's what we haven't talked about — the comments that actually matter.
'This video stopped me from doing something terrible tonight.' A real comment on a mental health post. 47 words that saved a life. No likes contest. Just reaching out.
'Your art is incredible. Don't stop.' 'I tried your recipe and my kids loved it.' 'This made me call my mom.' Small comments. Huge impact.
A negative comment is forgotten in a day. A kind one is screenshotted and re-read on bad days. One genuine comment keeps creators going for weeks.
After this post, go to your favorite creator's page. Leave one specific, genuine comment. Not 'nice.' Something real. Be the comment that matters. The internet is what we comment.

episodes.synopsis: After 24 episodes of terrible comments — the ones that actually change someone's day. Or life.
episodes.caption: 24 episodes of wild comments. The one that matters most? The kind one you leave today. Go comment something genuine. Tell me what you wrote 👇
